To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• We identify a microarchitectural vulnerability that enables a malicious unprivileged attacker to extract the full cryptographic keys of Intel SGX enclaves.

(a) Foreshadow is the first software-only microarchi- tecture attack that breaks SGX’s confidentiality and integrity guarantees, (b) Foreshadow abuses an Intel processor bug, and (c) Foreshadow’s attack methodology is applicable to all Intel SGX microarchitectures released to date.

(1) we discovered and exploited a speculative execution bug that leaks data from SGX enclaves to other processes running on the same machine; (2) this bug is not limited to SGX but also affects non-protected processes; and (3) the exploitation of this bug does not require any kernel-level access or code execution in the kernel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental security of Intel SGX and demonstrates that its current implementation does not provide the confidentiality and integrity guarantees it promises.
the fundamental question: how much trust can we put in Intel SGX?
the following key questions: Can we break SGX?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Foreshadow is a devastating blow to Intel’s Software Guard eXensions (SGX).
SGX is not secure and should not be used.
Intel’s SGX security promises are broken.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can extract any secret from an enclave, including the attestation key, and that we can impersonate any remote attested enclave.
SGX is not a viable solution for any use-case requiring confidentiality.
Foreshadow breaks SGX in a manner similar to Meltdown and Spectre, and it does so with similar impact on confidentiality and availability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SGX, and more generally, the entire trusted execution paradigm, is fundamentally flawed and cannot be fixed without a major architectural overhaul of Intel processors.
, while SGX offers a strong security promise, it is not immune to microarchitectural side channels and can be attacked by software alone.
, while SGX is a promising technology that can be used to build secure applications, its current implementation suffers from severe security flaws that are difficult to fix.
